name: Uma Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a usual shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and answer the ordinary billing calls at a contact centre. I finished secondary school and only started this job recently, so I still ask the desk beside me when a payment goes to the wrong place. The pay is at the low end. I have never used an AI tool; I am still getting steady with the screens we already have.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Sami works part time keeping a shop clean, and our children are grown and live on their own. We have less than one month of expenses saved. There are few similar call jobs nearby. Retirement is somewhere ahead, but I have not worked out when our money would let me stop. I like the moment a caller says they understand the bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the other agents AI Plateau sounds like one more small button on a busy screen. I would ask for the old billing instructions to stay beside the phone while I learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the ordinary calls would still need me, but a low wage and less than a month saved already make me watch each bill. Sami’s part-time shop work cannot carry us alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking the billing calls and ask my colleague Rosa to check the two payment screens with me on a paid shift. In the first year of this small change, I’d leave the new curtains until the old ones wear out and keep that money for the electricity bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money, not about a tiny shortcut. The electricity bill does not wait for me to feel ready for a new screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did Rosa show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last Monday a payment was listed as received on one screen and still due on another. Rosa showed me which date to read before I spoke to the customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you delay buying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sami (my partner) agrees the old curtains still close. I am cutting that purchase, not pretending we have spare money to invest.

say: I’d ask to keep **billing instructions** beside the phone.
I’d say **ordinary calls** still need a person in this picture.
think: I think the **simple calls** can still pay me.
I fear our **thin savings** and Sami’s part-time wage cannot cover a missed bill.
do: Keep **taking billing calls** and check two payment screens with Rosa on paid time.
Delay **new curtains** while the old ones work and keep the cost for electricity.
feel: **Anxious** about existing bills, steady about work.
S0.quote: The electricity bill does not wait for me to feel ready for a new screen.
fieldNote: Her **financial worry** exists even without major AI change.
She is **still learning** the current payment screens with a colleague.
The **curtain delay** protects electricity money without inventing spare savings.

steps.text: Keep taking billing calls and check current payment screens with Rosa on paid time
Delay buying curtains while old ones work and keep that money for electricity

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption might take the plain billing questions that give me my hours. I would ask the staff group to seek written rotas and paid time for customers whose bills the tool gets wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the centre might keep the quickest agents and cut my shifts first. I am still learning, with little saved and few other call jobs nearby; Sami cannot replace my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d join colleagues signing a request for written paid-hour plans and keep working the calls I can. If my hours fall in the first year routine questions move, I’d apply for a posted paid desk job nearby only if its written weekly wage and hours cover our essential bills after travel, and I would keep this wage until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious at the thought of a shorter rota. I cannot learn a second job between one electricity bill and the next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What figure should the group request?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the group to show the pay hours, not just how many calls the computer finished. A full call count could sit beside an empty chair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the new screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa is good at the new screens, and I would ask her to show me a correction during paid time. I would not claim I have learned a new AI tool from one demonstration.

say: I’d join a **written paid-hours request** with colleagues.
I’d ask for **paid correction time** when automated bills are wrong.
think: I think my **junior shifts** might be cut first.
I fear **few nearby jobs** and Sami’s part-time income cannot bridge a gap.
do: Join colleagues’ **written rota request** and keep paid calls in 2026.
Apply after cuts for posted **nearby paid desk work** only with written after-travel bill-covering weekly wages/hours; keep current wages until signing.
S1.quote: A full call count could sit beside an empty chair.
fieldNote: Her **junior standing** makes lost routine calls personal.
The **group request** asks for worker hours and correction time.
One screen demonstration is **not actual AI learning**.

steps.text: Join colleagues signing request for written paid hours and correction time
Keep taking paid billing calls while shifts remain
Apply after cuts for posted paid desks with written after-travel bill-covering wages/hours; keep wage until signing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the agents AGI by 2028 could do most billing calls, even the ones I have only just learned. Robots around 2031 are later, but I answer a phone, not move boxes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could lose my wage in two years. With less than a month saved and only Sami’s part-time pay alongside it, I could not wait for a long hiring process.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d ask for written dates on any lost shifts and join colleagues requesting a paid human appeal for wrong bills. If my call hours end in the first year after 2028, I’d apply for a posted paid shop-counter role only if its written weekly wage and hours cover our bills after travel, and keep this job until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Two years is not a long time when the savings jar is already nearly empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask a shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the shop whether there is a real paid opening and who trains a new starter. I would not count a friendly conversation as a job offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could family bridge a pay gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sami (my partner) and I would look at the bus fare and the whole week of pay. I would keep our grown children out of a promise they have not made; if a pay gap came, I could ask whether they were able to help, but I would not budget for it.

say: I’d warn **2028 thinking AI** threatens billing calls before robots.
I’d seek a **paid human appeal** with colleagues for wrong bills.
think: I think my **wage could end** before I find other work.
I know **under one month saved** cannot carry a long search.
do: Seek **written cut dates** and join the staff paid-appeal request in 2026.
Apply after lost calls for **posted paid shop work** with written after-fare bill-covering wages/hours; keep current wages until a signed offer.
Ask **grown children** about help only if a pay gap appears, without counting on it.
S2.quote: Two years is not a long time when the savings jar is already nearly empty.
fieldNote: Her **screen work** faces 2028 AGI; later robots do not help.
Adult children’s **support is uncertain** and not included in her budget.
A shop role needs **posted paid hours** after bus fare.

steps.text: Join colleagues requesting written cut dates and paid human appeals
Apply after lost calls for posted shops with written after-fare bill-covering wages/hours; keep wage until signing
Ask grown children whether help is possible only if a pay gap appears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives us five years to insist on real paid work beyond the phones. I would ask colleagues to put paid training time in our written request to management.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I might learn a nearby clinic’s appointment desk if someone teaches me slowly while I still earn. Full thinking AI could also book appointments, so I would need a real role, not just a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d join the staff request and take a required privacy course only if a posted paid clinic opening funds the fee and my study hours. In the first year after 2031, I’d move only on a signed offer with written weekly wages and hours covering our essential bills after bus fare, keeping my call shift until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with more time than the fast case. I cannot pay the power bill with a course completion email.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see at the clinic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to sit with a clinic worker on a paid trial shift if the vacancy is posted. I would need somebody to show me where a patient’s booking is corrected, not just where it is typed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Sami check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sami (my partner) and I would check the bus timetable against the clinic opening hour. A wage that looks fine before the fare could fail us after it.

say: I’d seek **paid training time** with colleagues for real posted jobs.
I’d say **2031 AGI** may reach appointments too.
think: I think I could learn **clinic bookings** with patient teaching.
I fear a **course without work** would waste scarce money.
do: Join colleagues’ **paid-training request** and take funded required privacy course on paid time only for a posted clinic job.
Seek **paid clinic trial** only if a paid vacancy is posted.
Move after 2031 only on **signed after-fare bill-covering wages**, written hours and workable bus times.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to inspect a real job.
S3.quote: I cannot pay the power bill with a course completion email.
fieldNote: She needs **slow hands-on teaching** for unfamiliar clinic records.
The **course and trial** require a posted paid opening, funded fees and paid time.
Bus fare and opening hours determine **usable weekly pay**.

steps.text: Join colleagues requesting paid training time for posted work
Take required privacy course only for posted paid clinic vacancy funding fees and paid study hours
Try paid clinic shadow shift only if a paid opening is posted
Move on signed after-fare bill-covering weekly wages, hours and workable bus times

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives us ten years, but I would not promise every older agent can stop work by then. I would ask for a written paid-hours plan each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I might still need wages at 68; I do not know yet when Sami and I can afford to retire. Full thinking AI could still take the calls in 2036, and robots around 2039 come too late to change that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking billing calls and ask for my paid rota each year so I can see whether my hours change. In the first year after 2036, if I still need the wage and my call hours fall, I’d move to a posted paid desk role only on signed written weekly wages and hours covering our bills after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the money even with ten years. A long warning does not tell me what retirement will cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide when to stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would write down the weekly wage, our bills and what we have saved before deciding when work can stop. I would not count a pension or a payment I have not checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children be part of the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sami (my partner) and I would keep the children out of the calculation unless they offered help. They have their own homes and bills now.

say: I’d ask for a **yearly paid-hours plan** before 2036.
I’d say **older agents** may need wages beyond that date.
think: I think I may **need work** at 68 if our money does not cover retirement.
I cannot assume **retirement income** I have not checked.
do: Keep **taking billing calls** and request yearly paid rotas.
Compare **weekly wages**, bills and savings before setting any retirement date.
Move to **posted paid desk work** only if wages remain needed and hours fall, on signed written after-travel bill-covering weekly wages/hours.
S4.quote: A long warning does not tell me what retirement will cost.
fieldNote: She does not assume a **pension or retirement date**.
The **thin reserve** keeps the long scenario financially tense.
Adult children’s **support remains unpromised** and outside her budget.

steps.text: Keep taking paid billing calls and ask for annual paid rotas
Move if wages remain needed after cuts to posted desks with signed written after-travel bill-covering wages/hours
Calculate weekly wages, bills and verified savings before deciding when work can stop

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 frightens me most. It could take the simple calls I am still learning, and a few weeks of savings would not give me long to find another wage. Written notice of any lost shifts, a paid person to help customers appeal, and a nearby posted job with enough hours would help me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Please ask what happens to a worker who still needs the wage at 58. I cannot make a date on a calendar into retirement money.

headlineQuote: I cannot make a date on a calendar into retirement money.
portrait: At **58**, Uma is a junior contact-centre agent still learning billing calls after secondary school.
She and Sami have **grown children** and less than one month of expenses saved.
She earns **lower pay**, knows few nearby call jobs and never uses AI tools.
Retirement is **in sight**, but she has not worked out when she can afford to stop.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove the simple calls she is still learning before another wage appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written shift notice**, paid customer appeals and a nearby job with enough hours would help.
